h1: Pricing a new seasonal beer against the core range
title: Pricing a Seasonal Beer vs Your Core | Craft Beer School
desc: How to price a new seasonal beer against your core range: real cost per litre, premium over core, pour size and when to end it.
teaser: Seasonals cost more to brew than your core beers. Price them as if they did.
standfirst: A seasonal beer gets regulars talking and brings lapsed drinkers back. It also costs more per litre than anything on your core list. Price it like a core beer and every seasonal batch quietly loses money. Here is how we would set it.
sections:
Your core beers benefit from scale and routine: full batches, bulk malt, the same hop bill every time and staff who know the process. A seasonal usually loses all of that. It may run as a half batch, use specialty malts at a higher price per kg, need extra hops for dry hopping or call for a fruit or spice addition.

Higher strength adds cost too. An 8% beer needs roughly twice the fermentable extract of a 4% beer, plus more yeast and longer tank time. Our guide to cost per litre shows how to build the full number, including the tank days that seasonal beers eat.
Work out the real cost of the batch

Cost the seasonal on its own, not as an average of the range. A worked example with round figures:

  • Core lager: ₹110 a litre in ingredients, energy and labour, brewed in 1,000 litre batches.
  • Seasonal hazy IPA: half batch of 500 litres, double the hops plus a dry hop, more malt for 6.5% ABV. Ingredients and labour come to ₹190 a litre.
  • Dry-hopped beers also lose more volume in the tank to hop debris, often several percent more than a clean lager. Add that loss to the cost of each litre you actually sell.

Your seasonal costs nearly twice what your core lager does per litre sold. If both sell at the same menu price, the seasonal earns far less per pour.
Set a premium over the core range

Drinkers expect a seasonal to cost a little more. A premium of 10 to 20% over your core range usually reads as fair. If your core pale ale sells at ₹340, a seasonal between ₹370 and ₹400 rarely raises eyebrows.

Check the margin at that price. At ₹380 for 400 ml, a beer costing ₹190 a litre has an ingredient cost per pour of ₹76. That still leaves a strong margin, close to your core beers. The premium is not greed: it keeps the seasonal earning its share of the rent.
Use pour size as a pricing tool

For strong or expensive seasonals, change the glass rather than the headline price. A 10% barrel-aged stout served in a 250 ml glass at ₹350 earns more per litre than a 400 ml pour at ₹420 and is a more sensible serve for the strength. Drinkers compare prices glass to glass more than per litre.

Print the pour size next to every price on the board. It is honest. It also stops the awkward moment when a guest who expected a pint receives a small glass and feels short-changed, which does more damage to a seasonal than any price.

Taster pours also help. A 150 ml pour of the seasonal on the tasting paddle lets cautious drinkers try it without committing to a full price glass.
Plan the end before the start

A seasonal should end on purpose. Decide in advance how many litres you will brew and what you will do with the last 10%. A seasonal that drags on for three months past its season at a discount teaches regulars to wait for the price to drop.

Time the next one too. A stream of two or three seasonals a year, each priced on its own cost, gives regulars something to come back for without cluttering the board.

Watch what each seasonal does to the core range while it is on. If your flagship pale ale sales drop by the same volume the seasonal sells, you have not grown. You have moved drinkers onto a beer that costs more to make. Price the seasonal so that this swap still earns you as much per pour. Then the risk disappears.
Check registration and label rules for new beers

In many states each new beer needs a brand or label registration with the excise department before it can be sold. The approval can take weeks. Factor that time and any fee into the plan. Rules vary by state and change, so ask the excise office or a licensing consultant what applies to your licence.

Reading cost per litre against margin per pour across a changing range is something brewers often find harder than the brewing itself. It is also the core of pricing a range that pays.
Cost your next seasonal before you write the recipe

Pricing works best when it starts with the recipe, not after the beer is in the tank. Our guide to beer pricing strategy covers the full approach.

Your first step: take your next seasonal recipe and cost it per litre sold, including batch size and tank losses. Put it next to your core beer's cost. That gap is your minimum premium.
faqs: How much more should a seasonal beer cost than a core beer?
A premium of 10 to 20% over the core range is common and usually reads as fair, but check it against the seasonal's real cost per litre.
Why do seasonal beers cost more to brew?
Smaller batches, specialty malts, extra hops, higher strength and longer tank time all raise the cost per litre sold.
Should strong seasonals be sold in smaller glasses?
Often yes. A smaller pour suits the strength and lets you hold a sensible headline price while earning more per litre.
